meta.title: Who really said "Whatever you can do or dream you can, begin it. Boldness has genius, power and magic in it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Goethe. The couplet is translator John Anster’s inventive 1835 paraphrase of a passage in Faust — the “Whatever” wording drifted in later.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Whatever you can do or dream you can, begin it. Boldness has genius, power and magic in it'?
meta.ogDescription: Goethe gets the credit, but the memorable English lines are John Anster’s 1835 free translation of Faust, not Goethe’s own words.

answer.label: Not Goethe — actually his translator, John Anster
answer.authorDates: 1793–1867 · Irish poet & first Briton to translate Goethe’s Faust
answer.sourceLine: The memorable couplet — “What you can do, or dream you can, begin it, / Boldness has genius, power, and magic in it” — was written by John Anster in his 1835 ‘very free’ English translation of Goethe’s Faust. It is an inventive paraphrase, not a line Goethe wrote; the popular “Whatever you can do” wording is a later drift. Quote Investigator concludes Anster — not Goethe — should be credited.

source.heading: The real source: John Anster’s 1835 Faust

docMeta.dd: Anster’s free English rendering of Goethe’s Faust, Part One (“Prelude at the Theatre”)

source.excerpt:
Are you in earnest? seize this very minute—
What you can do, or dream you can, begin it,
Boldness has genius, power, and magic in it.
trail: Quote Investigator concludes the distinctive 1835 couplet “should be credited” to translator John Anster — who was inspired by, but did not quote, Goethe’s Faust.
Wikiquote lists the line in its Misattributed section, noting the language traces to Anster’s translation rather than any line Goethe wrote.
Anster published ‘Faustus, a Dramatic Mystery’ in 1835 (Longman), the first British translation of part of Faust into English.
The “Whatever you can do” variant first appears in Marie Corelli’s 1905 essay, and Ralph Waldo Trine had already re-credited the lines straight to Goethe in 1897, per Quote Investigator.
source.excerptNote: Anster’s actual lines read “What you can do” (not “Whatever”) and place the couplet after “Are you in earnest? seize this very minute.” The widely shared “Whatever you can do” form is a later drift, and the prose passage (“Until one is committed…”) often attached to it belongs to mountaineer W. H. Murray (1951), not Goethe.

source.rightsNote: The couplet comes from John Anster’s translation of Faust, first published in 1835 — well before 1931 — so the English text is in the public domain in the United States. (Goethe’s German original, published 1808, is long public domain as well.)

author.name: John Anster
author.heading: Who was John Anster?
author.metaLine: 1793–1867 · Irish poet & Regius Professor of Civil Law, Trinity College Dublin
author.bio: John Anster was an Irish poet, lawyer, and academic who produced the first British translation of part of Goethe’s Faust into English (1835). Working in what critics called a ‘very free’ style, Anster often paraphrased rather than translated literally — and it was one such inventive paraphrase, the “Boldness has genius” couplet, that outlived his name and became the world’s most famous ‘Goethe’ quote he never wrote.

misattribution.heading: A translator’s words wearing Goethe’s name
misattribution.intro: This is a classic layered misattribution: a translator’s free paraphrase gets absorbed into the original author’s name, then reshaped and bundled with a third writer’s prose.

items.why: Goethe wrote a loosely related passage in the “Prelude at the Theatre” of Faust (1808), but not these words. Quote Investigator states plainly that “none of it was written by Goethe.”
Anster wrote “What you can do”; the swap to “Whatever you can do” is a modern drift, with the earliest known “Whatever” instance in Marie Corelli’s 1905 essay, per Quote Investigator.

items.scope: The “Until one is committed…” prose often quoted alongside it
items.why: The commitment passage frequently paired with the couplet was written by Scottish mountaineer W. H. Murray in The Scottish Himalayan Expedition (1951); Murray himself quoted Anster’s couplet at the end, and later readers mistook the whole block for Goethe (QI).

misattribution.truthLine: The memorable English lines are John Anster’s 1835 creation, inspired by — but not translated word-for-word from — Goethe’s Faust (Quote Investigator).

context.heading: Inspired by Goethe, written by his translator
lead: Goethe’s Faust opens with a “Prelude at the Theatre” in which a theatre manager urges the poet to stop deliberating and act. Goethe’s German is terse — roughly, ‘seize the possible boldly by the forelock’ — with no mention of genius, power, or magic.

When John Anster rendered the scene into English verse in 1835, he expanded the thought into a rousing couplet of his own invention. It was so quotable that it took on a life independent of both the play and its translator: by the late 19th century writers were crediting the lines directly to Goethe, and by 1951 they were fused with W. H. Murray’s prose on commitment.
context.pull: “None of it was written by Goethe.” — Quote Investigator
